title: Construction Job Pricing: Price Every Job for Real Profit
meta_description: How to price construction jobs for profit: work out true labour costs, cover waste and overheads, and hold a healthy net margin on every quote.
h1: Construction Job Pricing: Price Every Job for Real Profit
hero_subtitle: A step by step system for pricing jobs so the work you win actually pays.

intro.answer: Construction job pricing is not just covering labour and materials. It is understanding every cost, adding a proper profit margin, and protecting yourself with contracts that stop scope creep.

image.alt: A builder working through construction job pricing costs before sending a quote

intro.roadmap: This guide gives you a clear system for pricing that works in the real world. It covers calculating your true costs, building in a healthy margin, writing quotes that hold, and knowing when to say no to jobs that do not serve your business.

briefing.title: Build Every Price From Four Real Costs
briefing.intro: Most builders who underprice are not bad at maths. They are pricing from a day rate instead of from what the work actually costs them. Build the number up in the same order every time and the guesswork disappears.

panels.heading: What should a construction job price actually include?
paragraphs: Start with true labour cost, not the day rate. If you pay a carpenter £180 per day, then once you add National Insurance, pension, holidays, sick days and downtime, the real cost is closer to £220 to £240 per day.

Then materials plus at least 10 to 15% for waste, offcuts, damaged goods, supplier price rises and delivery. Then overheads, spread across the year: annual overheads divided by number of jobs. £60,000 of overhead across 30 jobs is £2,000 per job.

panels.heading: Build the number up in this order
paragraphs: Do these in sequence, every quote, and your margin stops being whatever is left over.
steps: True labour cost, including the on-costs and the downtime.
Materials, plus 10 to 15% for waste and delivery.
Overheads for this job: annual overheads divided by jobs per year.
Net profit on top, at 10 to 12%. Your wage is not your profit.

review.label: Check before you send
review.text: If the margin lands below 5%, it is not a job, it is a liability. If the scope is vague and the client will not sign a proper contract, do not touch it.
